Ancient Indian history

Indus Valley Civilization: facts for students

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilization, flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in its mature phase. It is known for planned cities with drains, standard brick sizes and weights, seals with an undeciphered script, and long-distance trade. Key sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Lothal.

We run day visits to Rakhigarhi and field visits to Dholavira and Lothal with archaeologists, for schools, colleges and adult groups.

Indus Valley Civilization: the basic facts

The civilisation is named after the Indus river, but its sites spread far beyond it: from Baluchistan to western Uttar Pradesh, and from Jammu down to Gujarat. More than a thousand settlements are known, most of them villages and small towns, with a handful of large cities. Archaeologists often prefer the name Harappan Civilization, after Harappa, the first site to be excavated in the 1920s.

Archaeologists divide it into three broad phases: Early Harappan (about 3300 to 2600 BCE), Mature Harappan (about 2600 to 1900 BCE) and Late Harappan (about 1900 to 1300 BCE). The famous features, such as standardised bricks and seals, belong to the mature phase. The roots go further back to farming villages like Mehrgarh in Baluchistan, occupied from about 7000 BCE.

  • Script: about 400 to 450 signs, written mostly right to left, still undeciphered.
  • Materials: copper and bronze, but no iron.
  • Bricks: fired and mud bricks in a ratio of roughly 1:2:4.
  • Weights: cubes of chert in a binary then decimal series.
  • Crops: wheat and barley, with millets and rice at some sites; cotton was grown and used.

Town planning and daily life

Harappan cities are famous for their planning. Many have a raised, walled area (often called a citadel) and a larger lower town. Streets often run roughly north to south and east to west, and houses open onto side lanes. Covered drains run along streets, and many houses had bathing areas and wells.

Daily life shows up in small things: clay toys, bangles of shell and terracotta, carnelian beads, spindle whorls for spinning thread, and grinding stones for grain. The seals, usually square steatite pieces carved with an animal and a short inscription, were probably used to mark goods and authority. No palace or royal tomb has been found, and how these cities were governed is still debated.

Major sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Lothal

Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are now in Pakistan, but India has many major sites, including the two largest Harappan settlements on Indian soil.

Rakhigarhi in Hisar district, Haryana, is one of the largest Harappan sites known, spread across several mounds beside a living village. It has early and mature phases and a cemetery. Our visit to Rakhigarhi, a Harappan city and a living village is the closest way to see a Harappan site from Delhi.

Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Rann of Kachchh, Gujarat, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021. It is built of stone, divided into a castle, a bailey, a middle town and a lower town, and is best known for its large rock-cut reservoirs that stored seasonal rain. Our field visit to Dholavira and Harappan urbanism in Kachchh looks closely at that water system.

Trade, crafts and contacts

Harappans worked carnelian, shell, faience, steatite and copper with great skill. Bead workshops at Lothal and Chanhudaro show long drilling processes. Mesopotamian texts mention a region called Meluhha that supplied carnelian, timber and other goods, and most scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region. Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf.

Lothal's large brick basin is often described as a dockyard; some archaeologists argue it was a water tank instead. Our programme on Lothal and its interpretations sets out both readings.

Why did the Indus Valley Civilization decline?

From about 1900 BCE the big cities shrank, writing and standard weights went out of use, and people moved towards smaller settlements, especially eastwards into Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. This is called de-urbanisation rather than collapse, because village life continued.

No single cause explains it. The evidence points to a combination: weakening monsoons and drier conditions, shifts in river courses including the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra system, and the breakdown of long-distance trade. The older idea of an Aryan invasion destroying the cities is not supported by the archaeology. Questions about who the Harappans were and how they relate to later populations are now studied with ancient DNA, and remain under active discussion.

Studying the Harappans in Delhi and beyond

The National Museum in New Delhi has one of the best Harappan galleries in India, with seals, pottery, jewellery and the bronze figurine often called the dancing girl. A museum morning with an archaeologist is a good first step before a site visit. For a wider view, see our Indian history timeline and the guide to famous archaeological sites in India.

Questions people ask

Who discovered the Indus Valley Civilization?

Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921 and R. D. Banerji began work at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. John Marshall, then Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924. Earlier visitors had noticed the Harappa mounds without recognising their age.

What is the largest Indus Valley site in India?

Rakhigarhi in Hisar district, Haryana, is the largest Harappan site in India and one of the largest anywhere. Its size estimate has grown as more mounds have been mapped. Dholavira in Gujarat is also large and is the best preserved stone-built Harappan city in India.

Why can't we read the Indus script?

Most inscriptions are very short, around five signs on average, and there is no bilingual inscription pairing the script with a known language, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian. Many decipherment claims have been made, but none has been accepted by most specialists.

Did the Harappans use iron?

No. The Harappans used copper, bronze, gold, silver and many kinds of stone, but not iron. Iron comes into wide use in north India later, in the late 2nd and early 1st millennium BCE.

Is the Indus Valley Civilization the same as the Saraswati civilisation?

Some writers use Indus-Saraswati or Sindhu-Sarasvati to stress the many sites along the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, which some identify with the Vedic Sarasvati. Indus Valley and Harappan remain the standard terms in most textbooks and research, and the river identification is still debated.
